Martin Luther King Jr. On August 28, 1963, standing at the steps of the Lincoln Memorial during the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, he delivered the defining oration of the American Civil Rights Movement. Its rhythmic cadence, biblical imagery, and repeated refrain became the rallying cry for a generation.

King held the nation to its own founding promise: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. He employed extended metaphors—the promissory note, the jailhouse of segregation—grounding moral urgency in familiar imagery. And he returned again and again to his vision: "I have a dream," he said, that one day his children would be judged not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.

The speech crystallized opposition to Jim Crow segregation and institutional racism, becoming the symbolic center of the Civil Rights Movement. Much of it was extemporaneous, particularly the final "dream" section, which drew on earlier King sermons. His vision of nonviolent resistance, shaped by Gandhian philosophy, made the Lincoln Memorial itself a monument to the movement's moral clarity.
